terms.gloss: his, her, its, their own; one’s own
evidence: Liv. 2.32.9: singulīs membrīs suum cuique cōnsilium, suus sermō
Plaut. Stich. 1.2.76: suus rēx rēgīnae placet, a queen likes her own king (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin’s “own” is the possessive itself: meus, tuus, noster, vester for the other persons, put first for weight (meā manū, with my own hand: Cic. Sen. 59).

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 21: tria praedia … propria trāduntur (Lewis & Short)
Phaedr. 1.4.1: āmittit meritō proprium quī aliēnum adpetit
terms.comment: The opposite of commūnis: what is yours alone.

evidence: Ter. Ad. 1.1.50: suā sponte rēctē facere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: meā, tuā sponte for the other persons; in good prose sponte always has the possessive (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: meī sunt ōrdinēs, mea dīscrīptiō, multae etiam istārum arborum meā manū sunt satae
phrases.english: the rows are mine, the plan is mine, and many of those trees were planted with my own hand

phrases.latin: singulīs membrīs suum cuique cōnsilium, suus sermō fuerit
phrases.english: each limb had its own mind and its own voice

phrases.latin: āmittit meritō proprium quī aliēnum adpetit
phrases.english: whoever grabs at what is another’s deserves to lose his own

proprius.against: Lewis & Short prō̆prius, marking the o both long and short
proprius.html: De Vaan 490, s.v. prō: short pro- occurs “in some older compounds, such as procul, probus, proprius”. The first syllable is heavy only by position, before pr.

sources: Lewis & Short: suus · Lewis & Short: proprius · Lewis & Short: sponte
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 490.
